The magnon corresponds to the higher-energy broadened peak (squares), the sharp weaker peaks below it originate from spurious Bragg scattering. The peak positions from the thermal-neutron data in a are also shown here for comparison (grey circles). (c) Raw energy scans across the upper magnon bands measured at several high-symmetry points using the PUMA spectrometer. Here the spectra are grouped and marked according to the small (original crystallographic) cubic Brillouin zone. (d) Individual energy cuts from the cold-neutron dataset in b for different momenta along (2 2 2-δ). The fits shown with solid lines neglect the spurious peaks at the low-energy side of the spectrum. The error bars in all panels represent 1 s.d. of the count rate.

Reciprocal lattice vectors 'a*' and 'b*' are shown, indicating the orientation of the reciprocal space.

Panel (c) provides a top-down view of the C8-BTBT molecular arrangement, with hydrogens and side chains omitted for clarity. It depicts two distinct molecular orientations, labeled 'M' (magenta) and 'B' (blue), stacking at an angle of "58°" relative to each other. To the right of these molecular arrangements, illustrations show three types of vibrational modes for a single molecule: a translational vibration in the π-π stacking direction (top row, purple arrows), a translational vibration along the short axis of the BTBT core (middle row, cyan arrows), and a libration mode along the long axis (bottom row, purple arrows). These molecular illustrations are connected by lines to three sets of grayscale square images on the right, which show simulated diffuse features for each vibrational mode.
*   Panel (d), corresponding to the top row of panel (c), shows three grayscale squares depicting simulated diffuse features for the translational vibration in the π-π stacking direction. *   Panel (e), corresponding to the middle row of panel (c), shows three grayscale squares depicting simulated diffuse features for the translational vibration along the short axis of the BTBT core.
*   Panel (f), corresponding to the bottom row of panel (c), shows three grayscale squares depicting simulated diffuse features for the libration mode along the long axis.

Panel (g) displays a simulated electron diffraction pattern that incorporates only the translational vibrational modes shown in panels (d) and (e). This grayscale image exhibits a clear diamond-shaped pattern of diffuse streaks, similar to the experimental pattern in (b). A blue dotted diamond overlay and an angle of "122°" are present, along with reciprocal lattice vectors 'a*' and 'b*'.

Panel (h) is a 3D surface plot illustrating the discrepancy (least square residual, R2) between the simulated and experimental diffraction data as a function of the amplitudes for the two dominant translational vibrations. The x-axis, labeled "σ_d", and the y-axis, labeled "σ_e", both range from 0 to 0.06. The z-axis, labeled "R2", ranges from 0 to 0.02. The surface shows a distinct minimum (colored blue) around σ_d ≈ 0.024 and σ_e ≈ 0.024, indicating the optimal amplitude values for the simulation.

Panel (i) shows a simulated electron diffraction pattern generated from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. This grayscale image also displays diffuse features and Bragg reflections, with reciprocal lattice vectors 'a*' and 'b*' indicated. The diffuse background appears somewhat broader and less defined than in panel (g).

Panel (j) presents an experimental electron diffraction pattern of C8-BTBT taken at a temperature of 100 K. This grayscale image shows distinct Bragg reflections, similar to panel (b), but with a noticeably reduced and fainter diffuse background compared to the room-temperature experimental pattern (b) and the MD simulation (i). Reciprocal lattice vectors 'a*' and 'b*' are shown.

Figure composed of atomistic/continuum simulation outputs comparing crack propagation in twin-free and nanotwinned aragonite.

Panels a–d: In-plane stress contour maps around an edge crack (white notch at left). Color bar at right spans −1.7 GPa (blue) to +1.7 GPa (red).
- a (label “T”): Twin-free single crystal with T-orientation at applied strain 3.75%. Localized stress concentration and a narrow red/blue process zone ahead of the crack tip.
- b (label “M”): Twin-free single crystal with M-orientation at applied strain 1.15%. Localized process zone with different shape/orientation relative to a.
- c: Nanotwinned aragonite at applied strain 6.8%. Alternating lamellae labeled T and M; multiple twin boundaries (TBs) incline across the field. Alternating compressive/tensile lobes (red/blue) indicate delocalized stress; the crack tip is blunted/trapped at a TB.
- d: Nanotwinned aragonite at applied strain 8.0%. Repeated T/M lamellae; stress alternation and blunted/crack-arrest behavior visible at several TBs.

Panel e: Stress–strain curves with legend:
- Black: Nanotwinned aragonite
- Red: Twin-free aragonite with T-orientation
- Blue: Twin-free aragonite with M-orientation

- “Crack propagates” on the red curve at low strain after the first peak.
- “Crack trapped by TB” on the black curve at low strain (corresponds to a plateau).
- “Crack penetrates through TB” on the black curve at higher strain (stress rises again before dropping).

- g: Nanotwinned case with a much larger transformed zone spreading across nanoscale twins; green and red outlines denote different transformed regions; domains labeled T and M; a black square marks a perfect-matrix reference region.

Voltage collapse occurs when these equilibria coalesce and the system trajectory diverges.

caption: Comparative dI/dV tunneling spectra of Bi(111) films with thicknesses of 4.0 nm, 8.0 nm, and 15.2 nm, measured under perpendicular magnetic fields ranging from 0 T to 11 T. The spectra, plotted against bias voltage (ranging approximately -130 mV to -20 mV), reveal three distinct Van Hove singularities (VHS) denoted as $E_V$, $E_{IV}$, and $E_{III}$. The features at $E_V$ (~ -105 mV) and $E_{IV}$ (~ -80 mV) exhibit no spectral shifting or splitting (indicated by vertical dashed red lines) regardless of magnetic field strength. Conversely, the $E_{III}$ peak (initially at ~ -55 mV at 0 T) undergoes pronounced Zeeman splitting into two resolvable peaks, labeled $E_{III, \uparrow}$ and $E_{III, \downarrow}$ (marked by diverging pink lines), with the splitting magnitude ($\Delta E$) proportional to the magnetic field strength, reaching approximately 21 meV at 11 T. Panel (c) includes higher-resolution field intervals (grey lines, 0.2 T steps). The 3D band structure diagram correlates these spectral features to specific topological points: saddle points at energies $E_{III}$ and $E_{IV}$, and a plateau at $E_V$ in the vicinity of the $\Gamma$ point. caption:
Composite analysis of the surface morphology and field-dependent electronic structure of a 4.0 nm thick Bi(111) film via Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) and Spectroscopy (STS). 

**Morphological Characterization:**
*   **Large-Scale Topography:** An STM image displays large, flat terraces separated by sharp step edges. An overlaid height profile (blue trace) traversing a step edge quantifies the step height at **4.0 Å**, corresponding to the Bi bilayer thickness. A white dot marks the spectroscopy acquisition site.
*   **Atomic Resolution:** A high-magnification scan reveals a highly ordered hexagonal lattice structure, confirming the crystallinity and (111) orientation of the film.

**Electronic Structure (Zero Field):**
*   **dI/dV Spectrum (B=0 T):** A tunneling conductance spectrum (plotted as dI/dV vs. Bias Voltage [-300 to +300 mV]) exhibits distinct electronic states labeled $E_I$ through $E_V$. Key features include:
    *   **$E_I$:** A sharp, pronounced peak at approximately **+210 mV**.
    *   **$E_{II}$:** A step-like edge feature near **+25 mV**.
    *   **$E_{III}$ - $E_V$:** A series of peaks in the valence band region located at approximately **-50 mV ($E_{III}$)**, **-75 mV ($E_{IV}$)**, and **-100 mV ($E_V$broad)**.
    *   A local conductance minimum is observed around +40 mV.

**Magneto-Spectroscopy and Landau Levels:**
*   **Field Evolution (0 T to 11 T):** A stacked waterfall plot of dI/dV spectra (bias range -150 to +150 mV) demonstrates the evolution of states under perpendicular magnetic fields ($B$).
    *   **Regime 0–5 T:** Spectra remain smooth, preserving the static peak positions ($E_{II}$–$E_V$).
    *   **Regime 6–11 T:** Oscillatory Landau Levels (LLs) emerge and intensify with increasing field strength. A distinct splitting of the **$E_{III}$** peak is observed (highlighted by diverging purple guide lines), indicating lifting of degeneracy or Zeeman splitting.
*   **SDLL Analysis (Top Trace):** The uppermost red trace represents the Second Derivative of the Landau-Level (SDLL) spectrum acquired at **11 T**. This derivative signal isolates high-frequency oscillations from the background. Vertical dashed grey lines establish a direct one-to-one correspondence between the peaks in the SDLL signal and the fine-structure oscillations in the 11 T dI/dV spectrum, confirming the quantization of states.

- Left vertical axis: Energy (meV), 0 to 70.
- Right vertical axis: Temperature (K), 0 to 145.
- Legend (symbols):
  - Black star: Band separation at 31 K (nematic band splitting).
  - Open black circle: Δ at 31 K (superconducting gap at 31 K).
  - Solid red circle: Tc.
  - Red open square: TA.
- Nematic order region (orange shaded) at low doping:
  - Black-star data (band separation) decrease with doping:
    - x ≈ 0.00 → ~50 meV (two labels near low x: “3 uc” and “50 uc (TA = 125 K)”).
    - x ≈ 0.02 → ~35 meV.
    - x ≈ 0.035–0.04 → ~20–25 meV.
    - x ≈ 0.05 → ~5–10 meV.

  - Gap Δ at 31 K (open circles) is finite within the dome, peaking around x ≈ 0.10–0.13 at ~9–10 meV, and going to ~0 by x ≈ 0.16.
  - Tc (red dots, right axis): low values near the left edge (~a few–10 K) rise to a maximum near x ≈ 0.11–0.13 at ~45–46 K, then decrease toward zero near x ≈ 0.16.

- Additional annotations on the left: “3 uc” near the top-left black star and “50 uc (TA = 125 K)” near a low-x point.

- Right schematic (heavily electron-doped): only blue electron pockets at the M points; no central hole pocket.

- Effective mass m*/me increases with electron doping in K-dosed FeSe and reaches higher values (~6–7) in Rb/K intercalated selenides near x ≈ 0.20.

raw_caption: Figure 1: Experimental set up and schematic lattice illustration. (a) Experimental arrangement. The crossed dipole trap beams propagate in the ex and ez directions. The static lattice is generated using the red beams with laser frequency ω, and moving lattice is generated using the blue beams with laser frequencies ω′ and ω′+δω. (b) Lattice potentials along the ex direction. The lattice period d is identical for the static lattice V0 and the moving lattice . The initial offset between lattice sites of the static and moving lattice, Δx, is dependent on the initial phase φ0 between the two lattices. The static lattice induces a large energy gap (I) through a two-photon process and a small energy gap (II) through a four-photon process. The moving lattice induces an energy gap when the s band and the p band are coupled through (III). A smaller energy gap is produced by a combination of the static and moving lattice (IV).

caption:
Multi-panel figure presenting the theoretical model, band structure, and transport properties of a tetragonal lattice slab representing a 3D topological insulator.

**(a) Lattice Model:** Schematic of a 3D tight-binding lattice model. Red spheres represent bulk atomic sites connected by blue cylindrical bonds. The slab is finite in the z-direction (10 layers) and infinite in x-y. The top layer features randomly distributed pink spheres representing surface vacancies (impurities).

**(b) Energy Dispersion:** 3D surface plot of the energy bands ($E$ vs $k_x, k_y$) for the clean system. A Dirac cone structure is evident at the $\Gamma$ point ($k=0$) where the conduction band (red) and valence band (blue) degenerate. Axis ranges: $k_x, k_y \in [-0.5, 0.5] \, \mathring{A}^{-1}$ and $E \in [-15, 15] \, \text{eV}$. An inset highlights the linear dispersion at the touching point.

**(c) Spectral Function:** Heatmap of the spectral function $-(1/\pi)\text{Im}[G(\mathbf{k}, \omega)]$ along the $\Gamma-X$ direction ($k_x$) versus energy ($\omega$) for impurity concentration $c=0.001$. The plot shows sharp, high-intensity (red, scale ~27 $\text{eV}^{-1}$) linear bands forming a V-shape centered at $k_x=0, \omega=0$, confirming the persistence of the Dirac cone structure under low disorder. Range: $\omega \in [-0.28, 0.28] \, \text{eV}$.

**(d) Conductivity vs. Fermi Level:** Line plot of DC conductivity $\sigma_{xx}(0)$ ($e^2/\hbar$) as a function of Fermi level $\mu$ (eV) for various impurity concentrations $c$.
- **Low Disorder ($c=0.002$, yellow curve):** Exhibits strong dependence on $\mu$, rising steeply from $\sim 0.05$ at $\mu=0$ to $>0.45$ at $\mu=0.29$ eV.
- **High Disorder ($c=0.2$, purple curve):** Shows flattened dependence on $\mu$, with higher conductivity at $\mu=0$ ($\sim 0.11$) compared to the clean limit, but lower conductivity at high $\mu$.
- **Crossover:** Curves for varying $c$ intersect, indicating a change in transport mechanisms.

**(e) Conductivity vs. Impurity Concentration:** Semi-log plot of $\sigma_{xx}(0)$ vs. $c$ at fixed $\mu=0.13$ eV. 
- **Trend:** Non-monotonic behavior.
- **Decay Phase:** Conductivity decreases rapidly from a maximum of $\sim 0.40 \, e^2/\hbar$ at $c \approx 5 \times 10^{-4}$ to a minimum.
- **Minimum:** The curve bottoms out at $\sigma_{xx} \approx 0.06 \, e^2/\hbar$ at a critical concentration $c \approx 0.006$.
- **Anomalous Increase:** Beyond the minimum ($c > 0.006$), conductivity rises steadily, reaching $\sim 0.24 \, e^2/\hbar$ at $c=0.5$, indicating an impurity-assisted transport regime.

Figure composed of five panels (a–e) illustrating spin relaxation under strong nonmagnetic disorder and associated simulation results.

a. Schematic of a single scattering event and spin precession.
- Vectors: k (initial momentum from origin O) and k′ (final momentum). The scattering-induced change is Δk (dashed arrow from k to k′).
- The electron spin σ (red) is shown misaligned with the new instantaneous effective magnetic field Beff (blue dashed arrow). A red tilted ellipse illustrates the precession of σ about Beff.

b. Multiple rapid scatterings and changing precession axes.
- Successive momentum changes Δk, Δk′, Δk″ (dashed arrows) are shown, each accompanied by a change of Beff (blue dashed) and a small-angle precession of σ (red ellipses).
- O marks the reference point.

c. Random-walk picture on the unit sphere.
- Circular boundary represents the unit sphere of spin directions.
- The spin direction evolves from σ(0) to σ(t) via a small change Δσ (dashed arrow), emphasizing that frequent scatterings lead to many small precession steps (a random walk), preserving the initial spin direction longer.

d. Numerical simulation: spin relaxation time τs vs momentum relaxation time τ at the Fermi level μ = 0.13 eV.
- Axes: x = τ (fs), range 0 to 6 fs; y = τs (fs), range 0 to 10 fs.
- Red open circles with a connecting red curve. τs is large at very small τ (≈8 fs near τ ≈ 0), drops to a minimum around sub-femtosecond τ, then increases with τ, reaching ≈10 fs at τ = 6 fs.

e. Simulated DC electro-spin susceptibility κyx(0) vs Fermi level μ for different impurity concentrations c.
- Axes: x = μ (eV), range ≈0.04 to 0.26 eV; y = κyx(0) (Å⁻1 V⁻1), range 0 to ≈0.12.
- Multiple colored curves labeled by c in the legend: c = 0.002 (black), 0.01 (light color), 0.02 (purple), 0.05 (yellow/green), 0.1 (orange), 0.2 (red). For all c, κyx(0) increases monotonically with μ.
- Inset: κyx(0) at fixed μ = 0.13 eV plotted against impurity concentration c.
  - Axes: x = c (from ≈0.001 to 0.1), y = κyx(0) (up to ≈0.08).
  - Red curve with points shows a nonmonotonic, U-shaped dependence with a minimum near intermediate c and larger κyx(0) at both low and high c.

Overall visual message:
- Frequent scatterings continually change Beff, causing spin to execute small-angle precession steps and a random walk in orientation.

raw_caption: Figure 4: Spin relaxation mechanism under high level of nonmagnetic disorder. (a) When scatterings are frequent, an electron suffers from rapid momentum change where the electronic spin does not have time to follow the instantaneous energy eigenstate given by adiabatic perturbation theory. Instead, the electronic spin precesses about the instantaneous energy eigenstate, which serves as an effective magnetic field Beff. (b) Frequent scatterings constantly change the precession axis of spin. During the interval of two consecutive scatterings the spin can only precess for a small angle. (c) The spin ends up doing a random walk on a unit sphere. The more frequent the scatterings are, the less efficient this random walk is, and consequently spin can preserve its original direction for a longer time. (d) The numerical simulation result for spin relaxation time and momentum relaxation time at Fermi level μ=0.13 eV. As expected, when disorder is high, and have an inverse dependence as in the traditional Dyakonov-Perel spin relaxation mechanism. (e) The simulated DC electro-spin susceptibility κyx(0) plotted against the Fermi level μ at different impurity concentrations. The inset is κyx(0) at a fixed Fermi level μ=0.13 eV versus impurity concentration c. It is clear that under high disorder, the accumulated spin density increases with impurity concentration.

raw_caption: Figure 7: Field-induced electronic dispersion for metals of different dimensionality. (a) The dispersion of Landau levels for a conventional three-dimensional metal placed in an external magnetic field applied along the z-direction. Owing to the underlying parabolic dispersion, each Landau level disperses quadratically as a function of kz, the momentum component along the applied field. Each partially occupied Landau level intersects the Fermi energy EF at two Fermi points, as indicated by the red dots. In the vicinity of the two Fermi points located at kz=±kF,n for the n-th partially filled Landau level, the quasiparticles disperse linearly with opposite group velocities v±,n=±ħkF,n/μ where μ is the effective mass. The ± signs of the group velocity respectively define the chirality of the right- and the left-moving one-dimensional fermions. (b) In contrast, for quasi-two-dimensional metals the Landau levels possess a periodic dispersion relation as a function of kz, owing to the tight binding term 2tc cos(kzd), with interlayer hopping strength and spacing, respectively, given by tc and d. Within the first Brillouin zone defined as -π/d<kz<π/d, each partially filled Landau level again gives rise to a pair of one-dimensional fermions of opposite chirality around the Fermi points. The situation depicted here corresponds to 4tc<ħωc, or when only one Landau level is partially filled. (c) Landau levels for 4tc>ħωc or when multiple Landau levels are partially occupied and each of them gives rise to a pair of chiral fermions.

caption:
Multi-panel figure illustrating electron-irradiation control of bulk conductivity in a 3D topological insulator (TI).

a) Schematic. A slab labeled “3D TI” is traversed by parallel electron-beam tracks (blue lines). Red dots inside the slab represent irradiation-induced point defects within the bulk. The graphic emphasizes that the beam penetrates the bulk while leaving the surfaces intact.

b) Calculated cross-section for Frenkel pair production. Plot of σ (barn) versus electron energy E (MeV) for three sublattices:
- Bi (blue curve)
- Te (red curve)
- Se (green curve)
Key visual features:
- Clear energy thresholds where σ first becomes nonzero: Se at the lowest E, Te at intermediate E, Bi at the highest E (Bi ≈ just above 1 MeV; Te ≈ around 0.6–0.8 MeV; Se ≈ around 0.3–0.4 MeV).
- At higher energies, σ(Bi) > σ(Te) > σ(Se). By E ≈ 2.5 MeV, σ values are approximately: Bi ~300 barn, Te ~120 barn, Se ~60–70 barn.
Inset cartoon shows an electron producing a displacement event that creates a Frenkel vacancy–interstitial pair (V and I indicated near a target atom), with the scattering geometry sketched.

c) High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM). Atomic lattice image of Bi2Te3; periodic spots are visible in the inset diffraction pattern. A white scale bar is present (text on the bar is too small to read).

d) ARPES spectrum after high-dose irradiation. Intensity map versus in-plane momentum k∥ (Å^-1) and energy E−EF (eV) showing a well-defined Dirac cone centered at k∥ = 0. Axes and annotations:
- Horizontal axis: k∥ from −0.2 to +0.2 Å^-1.
- Vertical axis: E−EF from −0.2 to +0.2 eV.
- Top annotation: “M → M” indicating the cut direction.
- The Dirac point label “EDP” appears on the left of the energy axis (numeric energy not printed on the panel).
Two horizontal dashed lines (yellow) mark approximate band edges visible in the map.

e) Dose-dependent resistivity and ambipolar conversion. Plot of longitudinal resistivity ρxx (mΩ·cm) versus electron dose φ (mC·cm^-2), with two data sets:
- Red squares: first irradiation ramp.
- Blue open circles: subsequent evolution (after thermal cycle / further irradiation).
Axes and annotations:
- x-axis: φ from 0 to 55 mC·cm^-2.
- y-axis (log scale): ρxx from 0.1 to 100 mΩ·cm.
- A prominent resistivity maximum occurs near φ ≈ 30–35 mC·cm^-2, reaching ~70–80 mΩ·cm.
- Left region labeled “p-type”; right region (gray shaded) labeled “n-type,” indicating a p→n conversion across the peak (charge neutrality point marked by a vertical dashed line).
- Inset cartoon band diagram: Dirac dispersion with EF crossing through the Dirac point ED; EF and ED are labeled.
- A secondary set of blue numbers along the top margin (30 to 65) is present without a visible axis label.

Overall, the figure visually demonstrates: (i) bulk defect creation by electron irradiation with element-specific σ(E); (ii) preservation of crystallographic order in TEM; (iii) robustness of the Dirac surface state in ARPES; and (iv) three-order-of-magnitude modulation of bulk resistivity with a clear p-type to n-type transition as dose increases.
raw_caption: Figure 1: Tuning bulk conductivity of topological materials by swift particle irradiation (a) Energetic electron beams can penetrate solids to a depth of many tens of micrometres. Electron irradiation affects the bulk but not the robust topological surfaces. (b) Impinging electrons induce formation of Frenkel vacancy-interstitial pairs (inset), which act to compensate the intrinsic bulk defects. Main panel: calculated crosssections σ for Frenkel pair production in Bi, Te and Se sublattices as a function of electron energy E, assuming displacement energy16 ∼25 eV. Energy thresholds, Eth, in σ are set by atomic weight; choosing or allows to tune Fermi level in both p- and n-type TIs. (c) Transmission electron microscopy image of Bi2Te3 with electron dose φ=1 C cm-2; the atomic displacements of ∼1 per 5,000 are not seen. Scale bar, 1 nm. (d) ARPES spectrum taken at 130 K (see 'Methods' section) of a Bi2Te3 crystal after irradiation with high electron dose of 1.7 C cm-2. The irradiated sample becomes n-type, with Dirac point at EDP=-290(10) meV relative to the Fermi level EF (just below the bottom of the bulk conduction band). It demonstrates electronic robustness of Dirac spectrum against electron irradiation. (e) Resistivity of p-type Bi2Te3 irradiated with 2.5 MeV electrons versus dose φ (red squares) measured in situ at 20 K shows about three orders of magnitude increase at the charge neutrality point (CNP) where the conduction is converted from p- to n-type, moving the Fermi level EF across the Dirac point (see cartoon). Cycling to room temperature reverses the process, which can be recovered by further irradiation (blue circles) and stabilized. The conversion from n- to p-type is obtained in a material such as Pb-based TI, where vacancies on the Pb sites are known to be of acceptor type.

Composite figure characterizing transport properties and quantum oscillations in Bi$_2$Te$_3$ across the charge neutrality point (CNP) induced by electron irradiation. 

**Transport Evolution with Irradiation Dose (Panels a, b):**
*   **Panel a (Top):** Longitudinal resistivity $\rho_{xx}$ (m$\Omega$ cm) vs. dose $\phi$ (0–100 mC cm$^{-2}$) at $T=4.2$ K. $\rho_{xx}$ exhibits a monotonic increase of three orders of magnitude from $\sim 0.1$ m$\Omega$ cm at $\phi=0$ (pristine) to a sharp peak of $\sim 50$ m$\Omega$ cm at $\phi \approx 89$ mC cm$^{-2}$, followed by a decrease at $\phi=99$ mC cm$^{-2}$. The background shading indicates a transition from p-type (white region) to n-type (grey region) conduction.
*   **Panel a (Middle):** Inverse Hall coefficient $1/(eR_H)$ ($10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$), representing carrier density $n_b$. The value decreases linearly from $\approx 7 \times 10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$ (p-type) at $\phi=0$ to near zero at $\phi \approx 89$, crossing to negative values (n-type) at $\phi > 90$, confirming the p-n transition.
*   **Panel a (Bottom):** Mobility $\mu$ ($10^3$ cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$) decreases from $\sim 11$ at $\phi=0$ to a minimum of $\sim 5$ near the CNP ($\phi \approx 80$), then recovers to $\sim 7$ in the n-type regime.
*   **Panel b:** Hall resistance $R_{xy}$ ($\Omega$) vs. magnetic field $\mu_0 H$ (-1 to 1 T) for varying doses. The slope $dR_{xy}/dH$ is positive for doses 0–89 mC cm$^{-2}$ (hole-dominated), reaching a maximum steepness at 89 mC cm$^{-2}$ (low carrier density), and inverts to negative slope at 99 mC cm$^{-2}$ (electron-dominated).

**Shubnikov-de Haas (SdH) Oscillations (Panels c-e):**
Oscillations of $\Delta R_{xx}$ (solid lines) and $\Delta R_{xy}$ (dashed lines) plotted against inverse magnetic field $1/(\mu_0 H)$:
*   **Panel c (0 mC cm$^{-2}$):** High-frequency oscillations indicating a large Fermi surface (schematic red circle). $R_{xx}$ and $R_{xy}$ are out of phase.
*   **Panel d (89 mC cm$^{-2}$):** Low-frequency oscillations indicating a significantly reduced Fermi surface size (small blue circle) near CNP.
*   **Panel e (99 mC cm$^{-2}$):** Frequency increases slightly relative to (d), corresponding to a growing electron pocket (purple circle).

**Band Structure and Hall Slopes (Panels f-h):**
Low-field $R_{xy}$ plots corresponding to samples in c-e. Insets show schematic band structures with Fermi level positions:
*   **f:** Linear positive slope; Fermi level in bulk valence band (BVB).
*   **g:** Steep linear positive slope; Fermi level at the BVB edge/Dirac point.
*   **h:** Linear negative slope; Fermi level in bulk conduction band (BCB).

**Berry Phase Analysis (Panel i):**
Landau level index $n$ vs. $1/(\mu_0 H)$ (Fan diagram):
*   **Pristine (0 mC cm$^{-2}$, Red):** Linear fit yields an intercept $\approx 0$, indicating a trivial Berry phase $\beta = 0 \pm 0.01$.
*   **Near CNP (89 mC cm$^{-2}$, Blue):** Linear fit yields an intercept of $\sim 0.5$, indicating a non-trivial Berry phase $\beta = 0.5 \pm 0.08$ characteristic of Dirac fermions.

**Schematics (Panels j, k):**
*   **j:** Before irradiation: Bulk conduction (yellow arrows) parallels surface states.
*   **k:** After irradiation (at CNP): Bulk is insulating (black), transport is dominated by topological surface states (arrows).

We note that in Bi2Te3, CNP and Dirac point do not coincide, with the Dirac point situated within a valley in the bulk valence bands5, and is expected to reflect that23. Magnetic field breaks time reversal symmetry and gaps Dirac bands, resulting in localizing behaviour shown as dash. Inset: optical image of the crystal showing van der Pauw contact configuration used. (b) Annealing protocol with time steps Δt=30 min implemented to tune Bi2Te3 crystal with dose 1 C cm-2 back to stable CNP. (c) Before annealing, the irradiated sample is n-type, with Dirac point at EDP∼-290(10) meV relative to the Fermi level EF. (d) After annealing at 120 °C, Dirac point upshifts to a binding energy of EDP∼-160(10) meV. The same shift is seen for the scans along Γ-M. (e) WAL low-field quantum interference correction to the linear-in-field magnetotransport ((f), also see text) at CNP in a Bi2Te3 crystal at 1.9 K with its characteristic low-field cusp. The 2D character of WAL is evident in its scaling with transverse field H‖=Hcosθ, where θ is the tilt angle of the field measured from sample's c axis. A fit to 2D localization (HLN) theory26 (solid line) confirms that the contribution is only from two surfaces and yields a dephasing field . (f) Linear magnetoresistance at CNP shows 2D scaling with H‖. (g) WAL contribution at CNP in a Bi2Se3:Ca(0.09%) crystal at 1.9 K also scales with H‖. At high fields outside the cusp, the scaling is seen to fail for θ≳60°. A fit to HLN theory (solid line) again confirms the contribution only from two surfaces and yields a smaller dephasing field Bφ∼0.004 T (corresponding to dephasing length lφ∼220 nm). Schematic and data plots detailing the conductive atomic force microscopy (c-AFM) writing and erasing of a nanowire at an oxide heterointerface. 

**Panel a:** Cross-sectional schematic of the sample architecture comprising a 3 unit cell (uc) LaAlO$_3$ layer (red), 100 nm SrTiO$_3$ layer (blue), and ~10 nm SiO$_2$ layer (grey) on a Si substrate. A c-AFM tip biased at $V_{\text{tip}} = +4$ V scans along the x-axis to create a conductive nanowire between two flanking electrodes.

**Panel b:** Real-time electrical conductance ($G$) measurement during the writing process shown in (a). 
*   **Axes:** Left Y-axis: $G$ (0.0 to 1.2 nS); Bottom X-axis: Position $x$ (0 to 70 $\mu$m); Top X-axis: Time $t$ (0 to 120 s).
*   **Dynamics:** The tip moves at 400 nm s$^{-1}$. Conductance remains at a noise floor near 0 nS until $x \approx 55 \mu$m, where it exhibits an abrupt, step-like increase to $>1.2$ nS, indicating the completion of the conductive path between electrodes.

**Panel c:** Schematic of the erasing process. The c-AFM tip, biased at $V_{\text{tip}} = -4$ V, scans along the y-direction (perpendicular to the wire axis) to locally sever the conductive channel.

**Panel d:** Conductance evolution during the erasing scan.
*   **Axes:** Left Y-axis: $G$ (0.0 to 1.2 nS); Bottom X-axis: Position $y$ (1.0 to 2.0 $\mu$m); Top X-axis: Time $t$ (200 to 400 s).
*   **Dynamics:** Scanning speed is 5 nm s$^{-1}$. The conductance starts high ($>1.2$ nS) and drops sharply to ~0 nS at $y \approx 1.85 \mu$m, confirming the wire cut.

Experimental data (blue triangles) are fitted with a sigmoidal function (black curve). The differential conductance ($dG/dy$, right axis, red curve) forms a Gaussian-like peak, centered at $y=0$, with a labeled Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of ~6.9 nm, representing the effective width of the erased junction.

caption: (a) Schematic representation of a generic 2D cavity consisting of an epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) host medium with cross-sectional area $A_h$ and permittivity $\varepsilon_h \approx 0$, enclosing a dielectric particle of area $A_i$ and permittivity $\varepsilon_i$. The system is bounded by a perfect electric conductor (PEC) wall, enforced by the boundary condition $\hat{n} \times E = 0$. (b) Numerical simulations of electric field magnitude distributions ($|E|$) for resonant eigenmodes in four topologically distinct cavities (I–IV). Each cavity comprises a silicon (Si) cylinder ($r_i=1.165 \, \mu m$) embedded in a silicon carbide (SiC) host. Despite extreme geometric variations—(I) amorphous non-canonical shape, (II) doubly connected annulus, (III) square, and (IV) high-aspect-ratio dumbbell—the cross-sectional area of the host $A_h$ remains constant ($49\pi \, \mu m^2$). Color maps show field localization (red/yellow) within the central dielectric inclusion, with varying field intensities in the surrounding host (blue/cyan) dependent on boundary proximity. (c) Dual-axis plot quantifying the electromagnetic response across the four geometries (I–IV). The left axis (red solid line) tracks resonance frequency normalized to the SiC plasma frequency ($\omega_{res}/\omega_p$), demonstrating approximate invariance with values stabilizing near 1.0 (deviation < 1.5%) despite geometric deformation. The right axis (blue dashed line) tracks the quality factor ($Q$), which exhibits significant dependence on geometry: $Q$ values fluctuate from a minimum of $\approx 225$ for the annulus (II) to a maximum of $\approx 255$ for the dumbbell (IV), highlighting that while eigenfrequency is topologically protected by the iso-areal condition, dissipative properties remain geometry-dependent.

Figure set showing inelastic light scattering from a LaAlO3 (LAO) crystal.

Panel a (LaAlO3 at 5 K, zero magnetic field):
- Plot type: Raman/luminescence spectrum; x-axis Raman shift (cm⁻¹) from 100 to 3,300; y-axis intensity (a.u.).

  - A1g peak in the low-wavenumber region.
  - Eg peaks in the low-wavenumber region.
  - L (luminescent transition) near ~290 cm⁻¹.
  - R (Raman modes) at ~1,100 cm⁻¹ (blue arrow) and in the high-wavenumber region around ~3,257 cm⁻¹ (green arrow) and ~3,281 cm⁻¹ (magenta arrow).
- The spectrum has a clear strong peak at ~1,100 cm⁻¹ and two weaker high-wavenumber peaks near ~3,257 and ~3,281 cm⁻¹.

Panel b (magnetic-field-dependent luminescent region):
- Plot type: Raman shift (cm⁻¹) 250–320; y-axis intensity (a.u.).
- Field dependence: stacked spectra from 0 T (bottom) to 9 T (top) in 1 T increments (Δ = 1 T, arrow at left).
- Colored arrows mark field-split components near ~271 cm⁻¹ (olive/orange arrows) and ~290 cm⁻¹ (purple arrows).
- Observation: increasing magnetic field produces clear Zeeman splitting of these luminescent features; split components move apart symmetrically with field.

Panel c (magnetic-field-dependent Raman mode near 1,100 cm⁻¹):
- Plot type: Raman shift (cm⁻¹) 1,080–1,140; y-axis intensity (a.u.).
- Field dependence: spectra from 0 T to 9 T in 1 T steps (same stacking as b).
- A Raman mode at ~1,100 cm⁻¹ (blue arrow) splits under field into multiple components (visible triplet-like splitting), with separation increasing with magnetic field.

Panel d (third-order Raman region):
- Plot type: Raman shift (cm⁻¹) 3,240–3,300; y-axis intensity (a.u.).
- Field dependence: spectra from 0 T to 9 T in 1 T steps.
- High-wavenumber features around ~3,257 cm⁻¹ (green arrows) and ~3,281 cm⁻¹ (magenta arrows) show magnetic-field-induced splitting similar to panel c; these are identified as third-order features of the ~1,100 cm⁻¹ Raman mode.

Panel e (temperature dependence of split-line intensity vs hysteresis loop shift):
- Plot type: x-axis temperature (K) from 0 to ~125.
- Left y-axis: Intensity (a.u.) of magnetically split components; symbols identify five features:
  - 271 cm⁻¹ (olive circles)
  - 290 cm⁻¹ (purple triangles)
  - 1,109 cm⁻¹ (blue squares)
  - 3,257 cm⁻¹ (black diamonds)
  - 3,281 cm⁻¹ (gray pentagons)
- Right y-axis: μ0Hshift (mT) of an LSMO/LAO/LSMO stack (red curve).

  - All five intensities are largest at low temperature and decrease monotonically with increasing temperature, approaching near-zero above ≈100–120 K.

- LAO exhibits both Raman and defect-related luminescent features that Zeeman split under an applied magnetic field up to 9 T.

- The temperature dependence of the split-line intensities mirrors the temperature dependence of the magnetic hysteresis loop shift measured in an LSMO/LAO/LSMO structure, indicating correlated magnetic-field-sensitive excitations in LAO.

Panel a (upper-left): false-color 2D map (Δp on x, Δs on y) of P2 with a diagonal, stretched, high-population ridge of high values (red → yellow → green) running from the top-left toward the bottom-right, and a narrow, nearly vertical bright stripe at the far right near Δp ≈ +115 MHz. Background is dark blue (near 0). Colorbar indicates maximum ≈0.9.

Panel b (middle-left): false-color 2D map (same axes) of P1 showing a complementary structure — a vertical high-population stripe near Δp ≈ 0 (bright band) and distortions near Δs ≈ 0 where a low-P1 (dark) region intersects. The diagonal region corresponding to the P2 bright ridge in (a) appears as low P1 (dark), forming a “dark resonance” locus. A narrow feature near Δp ≈ +115 MHz is also visible.

Panel c (upper-center/right): false-color 2D map of P2 (theoretical) with a very similar diagonal bright resonance from top-left to bottom-right and the same narrow vertical high-P2 feature at Δp ≈ +115 MHz. Color scale again ranges to ≈0.9.

Panel d (middle-center/right): false-color 2D map of P1 (theoretical) showing the expected low-P1 (dark) diagonal “dark resonance” where P2 is high, a vertical bright band near Δp ≈ 0, and a split/structure near Δs ≈ 0.

Panel e (top-right narrow plot): line plot of P2 versus Δp / 2π (MHz) with the annotation “Δs = 0” printed on the panel. Blue experimental data points connected by markers show a broad main peak centered near Δp ≈ 0 reaching about 0.8–0.9 and a narrow, high, secondary peak near Δp ≈ +115 MHz that reaches the top of the plotted scale (~0.9). Overlaid solid and dashed curves (calculated/simulated traces) closely follow the experimental markers for the main peak; small discrepancies occur at the right-side narrow peak.

Panel f (bottom-right narrow plot): line plot of P1 versus Δp / 2π (MHz) with the annotation “Δs = 0.” Green experimental markers show a pronounced dip (low P1) near Δp ≈ 0 (P1 nearly zero) corresponding to the dark resonance, several smaller structure/peaks at other detunings, and a noticeable peak cluster around Δp ≈ +115 MHz where P1 rises to roughly 0.2–0.3. - A diagonal bright resonance in P2 maps (a, c) extending from top-left to bottom-right consistent with a two-photon resonance locus.
- A corresponding dark (low-P1) diagonal region in P1 maps (b, d) where P2 is large.
- A distinct narrow vertical high-P2 feature near Δp ≈ +115 MHz visible in a, c and in line plots e,f (right-side narrow peak), and a vertical stripe near Δp ≈ 0 in P1 maps (resonant excitation of P1).

Multi-panel figure (labeled a–c) illustrating STIRAP pulse shapes and measured level populations versus time for a three-level system.

Panel a (pulse envelopes):
- Y-axis: Ωs,p(t)/Ω0 (normalized Rabi amplitudes).
- X-axis: t (ns), spanning approximately −300 to +300 ns with ticks at −300, −200, −100, 0, 100, 200, 300.
- Two smooth pulses:
  - The Stokes pulse Ωs/Ω0 (left-peaked curve) rises from ~0 near −300 ns, reaches its maximum (~1.0) around −70 to −100 ns, then decreases toward 0 by +300 ns.
  - The pump pulse Ωp/Ω0 (right-peaked curve) is time-reversed relative to Ωs: it is small at −300 ns, crosses the Stokes pulse near t ≈ 0 where their amplitudes are equal, peaks (~1.0) around +70 to +100 ns, and returns to ~0 by +300 ns.
- The two pulses are of similar shape and amplitude, with a “counterintuitive” ordering (Stokes-first, pump-second).

Panel b (measured populations):
- Y-axis: P0,1,2 (state populations), scale from 0 to ~1.1 (tick at 1.0 shown).
- X-axis: t (ns), −300 to +300 (same ticks as panel a).
- Three time traces:
  - P0 (red, square markers/line): near 1.0 for t ≤ −100 ns; drops steeply around t ≈ 0; settles near ~0.05–0.1 for t ≥ +100 ns.
  - P2 (blue, triangle markers/line): near 0 at early times; rises steeply around t ≈ 0; plateaus at ~0.8–0.9 for t ≥ +100 ns (approximately 0.85 by eye).
  - P1 (green, circle markers/line): remains low throughout, with a small transient bump around t ≈ +20 to +60 ns staying well below 0.1.
- The transition from P0 to P2 occurs mainly within ±50 ns of t = 0, with P1 remaining small.

Panel c (corrected/compared populations):
- Axes identical to panel b.
- Three traces with symbol markers overlaid by smooth lines (symbols represent data; smooth lines represent a close-fitting model/guide):
  - P0 (red, squares): decreases from ~1.0 to near 0 across t ≈ 0; final level slightly above 0 (~0.02–0.05).
  - P2 (blue, triangles): increases from ~0 to a higher plateau than in panel b, approaching ~0.95–0.98 for t ≥ +100 ns.
  - P1 (green, circles): remains near 0 with a small, narrow transient hump below ~0.05 around t ≈ 0–50 ns.
- The symbols and lines closely overlap across the full time range, indicating very good agreement.

Key visual takeaways:
- Counterintuitive pulse sequence (Stokes precedes pump) with equal crossing at t ≈ 0.
- Efficient population transfer from |0> to |2> while |1> remains weakly populated.
- Panel b shows a final P2 near ~0.85; panel c shows an improved final P2 near ~0.97, with minimal residual P0 and very small transient P1.

Plots characterizing the temperature-dependent electrical resistivity of 1T′-MoTe$_2$ at ambient pressure. 

**a) Broad Temperature Range (0–300 K):**  
Resistivity exhibits semimetallic behavior, decreasing monotonically from $\approx 10.5 \times 10^{-6} \, \Omega \, \text{m}$ at 300 K as temperature lowers. A distinct thermal hysteresis is observed between the cooling (black) and warming (red) curves. 
- **Inset (200–290 K):** Detailed view of the first-order structural phase transition (1T′ to Td). The cooling curve displays a local resistivity anomaly (peak) at $\sim 250$ K. The warming curve traces a lower resistivity path, closing the hysteresis loop at $\sim 280$ K. The inset y-axis (labeled 0.8–1.2) captures the topological features of the transition, though absolute magnitudes correspond to the $\sim 10 \times 10^{-6} \, \Omega \, \text{m}$ scale of the main plot.

**b) Low Temperature Regime (0–1.2 K):**  
Zoomed view identifying the superconducting transition. 
- **Normal State:** Resistivity decreases slightly from $\approx 0.37 \times 10^{-6} \, \Omega \, \text{m}$ at 1.2 K to $\approx 0.28 \times 10^{-6} \, \Omega \, \text{m}$ at 0.3 K.
- **Transition:** A sharp superconducting onset is visible at $T_{onset} \approx 0.25$ K.
- **Zero Resistance:** The curve reaches a zero-resistance state ($R=0$) at the critical temperature $T_c = 0.10$ K.

Figure with three panels summarizing high-pressure behavior of 1T′-MoTe2.

Panel a (Raman spectra):
- Sample: MoTe2; measurement: Raman intensity (arb. units) vs Raman shift (cm−1).
- X-axis range: 150–350 cm−1.
- Five spectra recorded at room temperature under different pressures:
  - 0.8 GPa (red)
  - 3.5 GPa (green)
  - 8.8 GPa (dark blue)
  - 14.8 GPa (light blue)
  - 21.2 GPa (magenta)
- Each spectrum shows two prominent peaks associated with 1T′ vibrational modes:
  - Lower-frequency peak (Bg) near ~170–200 cm−1, shifting to higher wavenumber with pressure.
  - Higher-frequency peak (Ag) near ~260–300 cm−1, also shifting upward with pressure.
- No new peaks or discontinuities appear across the pressure range.

Panel b (Raman peak positions vs pressure):
- Y-axis: Raman shift (cm−1) from 150 to 350.
- X-axis: Pressure (GPa) from 0 to ~35.
- Two datasets:
  - Bg mode (black squares): increases approximately linearly from ~170 cm−1 at 0 GPa to ~215 cm−1 at ~35 GPa.
  - Ag mode (red circles): increases from ~255–260 cm−1 at 0 GPa to ~315–320 cm−1 at ~35 GPa.
- The pressure dependence is smooth and continuous for both modes; no discontinuities are visible.

Panel c (monoclinic angle β vs pressure):
- Y-axis: monoclinic angle β (degrees) ranging from 90 to 96.
- X-axis: Pressure (GPa) from 0 to 2.
- Three datasets:
  - 295 K (room temperature, red filled squares): β increases gradually with pressure, from ~94.2° at 0 GPa to ~95.5° at 2 GPa.
  - 135 K, compression (blue filled circles): β ~90–91° at low pressure, then exhibits a sharp jump to ~94° at ~0.8 GPa; above ~0.8 GPa, β continues to rise slightly with pressure, approaching ~95° near 2 GPa.
  - 135 K, decompression (blue open circles): β remains ~94–95° down to ~0.8 GPa, then drops abruptly to ~90–91° near ~0.4 GPa, indicating reversible Td ↔ 1T′ transition with hysteresis.
- Overall, increasing pressure at room temperature enhances monoclinic distortion (larger β). At 135 K, a first-order transition occurs with different thresholds on compression (~0.8 GPa) and decompression (~0.4 GPa).

caption:
Figure composed of five left-hand hysteresis panels (a–e) and four right-hand schematic magnetization-stage illustrations (f–i).

Left column – hysteresis/XMCD panels:
- Common x-axis for all panels: μ0H (mT) from −200 to +200 with major ticks at −200, −100, 0, +100, +200. A vertical solid line marks H = 0 mT. Four red dashed vertical lines mark representative field positions associated with the schematics (labels i, h, g, f aligned near the top of panel a).
- Panel a (top): labeled "VSM" at upper-left. y-axis labeled M/MS with tick values −1, 0, +1. The VSM hysteresis shows a two-step loop: near-saturation at +1 for large positive fields, a subloop/shoulder region around positive intermediate fields, and a switch through M = 0 to −1 at negative fields. Two close-overlapping traces are plotted (two similar black curves).
- Panel b: labeled "Gd". y-axis labeled "XMCD asymmetry (normalized units)" and range −1 to +1. The Gd XMCD loop shows positive asymmetry at large positive μ0H and a relatively sharp reversal through zero toward negative asymmetry as field is swept negative. Two similar traces are shown.
- Panel c: labeled "Fe". Same y-axis scale. The Fe loop is opposite in sign to Gd (negative asymmetry at large positive fields, crossing to positive at negative fields), indicating antiparallel alignment relative to Gd. Two traces present.
- Panel d: labeled "Co". Same y-axis scale. The Co XMCD loop displays a non-monotonic dip–bump–dip structure around low fields (features straddling H = 0), indicating complex reversal behavior. Two traces are shown.
- Panel e: labeled "Ni". Same y-axis scale. The Ni XMCD also shows a non-monotonic multi-feature structure (dip–peak–dip) near low fields and broader changes toward positive fields. Two traces are shown.

Approximate positions of the red dashed vertical lines (fields associated with the schematics):
- leftmost dashed (labeled i): ≈ −150 mT;
- next dashed (labeled h): ≈ −30 to −50 mT;
- next dashed (labeled g): ≈ +80 to +100 mT;
- rightmost dashed (labeled f): ≈ +180 to +200 mT.

Center legend (between panels and schematics):
- Small boxed legend showing colored arrows with labels: black arrow labeled "Gd"; purple arrow labeled "Fe"; yellow/orange arrow labeled "Rotatable NiCo"; grey arrow (uncolored box) and red arrow labeled "Pinned NiCoO" (legend identifies distinct arrow colors used in the schematics to denote element- and region-specific magnetization directions).

Right column – four 3D schematic block illustrations showing layer stack and magnetization at selected stages (panels f–i, arranged top to bottom):
- Common features: a large right-pointing arrow at top labeled "Cooling and applied field +H". Each schematic shows a layered block (top to bottom): green layer (GdFe), a thin white/grey interfacial mixture layer, a blue layer (NiCo), and a dark grey/black bottom layer (NiCoO). Colored small arrows inside each layer indicate local magnetization directions using the same color code as the legend (black for Gd, purple for Fe, orange for rotatable NiCo, grey and red for pinned NiCo/NiCoO).
- f (top schematic, labeled f): at high positive applied field. Black arrows in the green GdFe layer point to the right (parallel to +H); purple Fe arrows in that layer point left (antiparallel to Gd). Orange arrows in the blue NiCo layer point right; in the dark NiCoO region multiple small red/grey arrows show pinned moments oriented largely to the right.
- g (second schematic): at reduced positive field. Gd (black) arrows remain largely right; Fe (purple) remain left. Orange rotatable NiCo arrows in the blue layer are reversed (point left) relative to panel f. Pinned moments (grey/red) in the NiCoO remain oriented similar to f.
- h (third schematic): at small negative applied field. Black Gd arrows have switched to point left; purple Fe arrows have switched accordingly (now pointing right relative to Gd); orange rotatable NiCo arrows in the blue layer point left (aligned antiferromagnetically relative to Gd in this stage); pinned NiCoO moments remain unchanged.
- i (bottom schematic): at large negative field. Gd/Fe orientation remains reversed relative to f; orange rotatable NiCo arrows in the blue layer now point right again (parallel to the GdFe in this stage); pinned NiCoO moments remain oriented as shown in previous schematics.

Overall visual information conveyed:
- Element-specific XMCD loops (Gd, Fe, Co, Ni) are plotted vs μ0H (−200 to +200 mT) with normalized asymmetry (−1 to +1). Gd and Fe loops are opposite in sign (ferrimagnetic alignment). Co and Ni loops show complex non-monotonic features (dip/bump/dip) near low fields. The VSM loop (panel a) shows a two-step-like hysteresis with subloop features; four vertical dashed field markers indicate the four schematic magnetic configurations (i, h, g, f). The layer stack and colored arrows in schematics indicate relative orientations of Gd, Fe, rotatable NiCo and pinned NiCoO at those marked fields.

Axes: x from −300 to +300 mT (μ0H); y in magnetic moment m (μemu) from approximately −100 to +200 μemu.
- Color scale: red (300 K) to blue (420 K).

- Phase 1 (labels on plot): HE(Phase 1) ~ constant small positive value (~+5–10 mT) from 300 K to ~350 K; HC(Phase 1) small (a few mT) and decreases with T; both vanish when phase 1 disappears above ~350 K.

raw_caption: Figure 1: Encoded superconducting qubits and tunable Josephson junctions. (a) Schematic diagram of a possible encoded superconducting qubit scheme as described in the text. An encoded qubit consists of two tunable physical SC qubits (for example, tunable transmons such as the xmon depicted here), with the encoded qubit states |0〉Q=|01〉 and |1〉Q=|10〉. In this picture, two encoded qubits are shown (for example, physical qubits 1a and 1b form an encoded qubit) and more encoded qubits can be introduced in a straightforward manner. Each SC qubit has a z-control line which tunes the Josephson energy EJ, and there are no additional microwave xy-control lines. All manipulation of the qubit states are done by the z-control pulses. Each transmon is capacitively-coupled to neighbouring transmons and also coupled to, as an example, a transmission line resonator for readout. (b) Double JJs in a loop act as a tunable JJ, controlled by an externally applied magnetic flux. In the SQUID tunable approach, one of the transmons in each encoded qubit needs a separate voltage control to tune the gate charge number ng which may be needed to initialize the encoded qubit state. (c) electrostatically tunable JJ on the basis of a proximitized superconducting-semiconductor nanowire connecting two superconductors30 used for gatemons. The nanowire is coated with SC and a portion is lifted off to form a semiconductor nanowire weak link. The JJ energy EJ is tuned by a side-gate voltage VG, which can also serve as a capacitive tuning for initialization.
